reigns.tagline: The Frankish king who brought back the Roman emperor
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Pippin the Short, king of Franks
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned by Pope Leo III in Rome
reigns.previously: No emperor in the West for over 300 years. The Franks rule instead.
paragraphs: By 800 Charles, king of the Franks, already ruled most of western Europe. He had spent thirty years at war, above all against the pagan Saxons, whom he beat, baptised by force and punished brutally. He had swallowed the Lombard kingdom of Italy too. Then Pope Leo III, beaten up by Roman rivals, came to him for help. Charles marched to Rome to put him back on his throne.

On Christmas Day 800, as Charles prayed in St Peter's, Leo set a crown on his head and the crowd hailed him as emperor of the Romans. For the first time in over three centuries the West had an emperor again. From his palace at Aachen he pulled scholars from all over Europe, had old Latin books copied in a clear new handwriting, and ordered schools at monasteries and cathedrals.

He outlived most of his sons. In 813, at Aachen, he crowned his last surviving legitimate son Louis as co-emperor himself, with no pope involved. A few months later, in January 814, he caught a fever, then pleurisy, and died at about 66.

claims.text: Charlemagne had no idea the pope was going to crown him.
claims.note: His biographer Einhard says he would never have entered the church that day had he known. Many historians think the scene was planned and the protest was modesty for show.

claims.text: He never really learned to write.
claims.note: Einhard says he kept writing tablets under his pillow to practise at night but started too late in life. He could read and spoke Latin well.

claims.text: He had 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded in one day at Verden in 782.
claims.note: The Royal Frankish Annals give the figure. Some historians suspect a copying error or exaggeration; nobody doubts a mass killing happened.

reigns.hook: The old emperor is dead and the whole empire passes to one man. Louis is serious, devout and has three grown sons of his own. Every one of them is already counting his share.

reigns.tagline: The emperor his own sons dethroned, twice
reigns.previously: Charlemagne dies at Aachen, after crowning his son Louis himself.
paragraphs: Louis cleaned house fast. He threw his party-loving sisters out of the palace and filled the court with monks and reformers. In 817 he made his eldest son Lothair co-emperor and gave the younger two smaller kingdoms. His nephew Bernard, king of Italy, rebelled; Louis had him blinded, and Bernard died of it. In 822 the guilt-stricken emperor confessed his sins in public at Attigny.

Then his second wife Judith gave him another son, Charles, in 823. Making room for the boy meant cutting the older sons' shares, and they rose against him. In 833, near Colmar, Louis's army simply melted away to his sons. Lothair had him deposed and forced to do penance in church as a sinner unfit to rule.

The brothers soon fell out, and in 834 Louis was back on the throne. He spent his last years juggling his sons' shares again. He died in June 840 on an island in the Rhine, with his sons still at odds.

claims.text: The place where his army deserted him became known as the 'Field of Lies'.
claims.note: Writers sympathetic to Louis, such as the Astronomer and Nithard, record the name, blaming the sons' broken promises.

claims.text: Empress Judith was having an affair with the chamberlain Bernard of Septimania.
claims.note: The charge came from the rebels and their supporters. It suited them perfectly; there is no independent proof.

claims.text: A total eclipse of the sun in May 840 frightened him into his final illness.
claims.note: The eclipse really happened and the Astronomer mentions it near his death. Making it the cause is a later dramatic touch.

reigns.hook: Louis is dead. Lothair says the whole empire is his, as promised back in 817. His brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald say otherwise, and they're raising armies.

reigns.tagline: He wanted it all, and the empire got split in three
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Eldest son of Louis the Pious
reigns.previously: Louis the Pious dies. Three sons, one empire, no agreement.
paragraphs: Lothair claimed the lot. His brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald joined forces, and on 25 June 841 the Franks fought each other at Fontenoy, near Auxerre. It was a slaughter and Lothair lost. In 842, at Strasbourg, Louis and Charles swore loyalty to each other in front of their armies, each in the other army's own language so every soldier understood.

Worn out, the three made peace at Verdun in August 843. Charles took the west, the seed of France. Louis took the east, the seed of Germany. Lothair kept the imperial title and a long middle strip from the North Sea through Aachen and Burgundy down to Italy. That middle strip would be fought over for a thousand years.

In 855, sick and ageing, Lothair split his kingdom between his three sons, then entered the abbey of Prüm as a monk. He died there six days later. His eldest son Louis, already ruling Italy, kept the crown of emperor.

claims.text: The Oaths of Strasbourg are among the oldest surviving texts in early French and German.
claims.note: The historian Nithard, Charles's cousin, copied the oaths word for word into his history, in both languages.

claims.text: Fontenoy killed so many Frankish nobles that the kingdoms couldn't fight off the Vikings afterwards.
claims.note: Chroniclers and the poet Angelbert describe terrible losses, but no reliable numbers survive and later historians doubt the long-term effect.

claims.text: Lorraine is named after his family.
claims.note: His son Lothair II got the northern part of the middle kingdom, called Lotharingia, 'Lothair's realm', which became Lorraine.

reigns.hook: The new emperor is a Carolingian who barely leaves Italy. Arab raiders are loose in the south, and they have already sacked St Peter's in Rome. Louis means to drive them out.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who never left Italy, and once got locked up
reigns.previously: Lothair I dies a monk. His sons split his middle kingdom three ways.
paragraphs: Louis II was an emperor whose empire was really just Italy. Arab raiders from North Africa and Sicily had set up an emirate at Bari, on the heel of Italy, and in 846 a raiding fleet had looted St Peter's itself. Louis made fighting them his life's work, campaigning year after year in the south.

In 871, with help from a Byzantine fleet, he finally took Bari and captured its emir. Weeks later he was the captive. Prince Adelchis of Benevento, fed up with Frankish troops on his land, seized Louis at Benevento and only let him go after he swore never to take revenge. The pope later freed him from the oath.
He also traded angry letters with the Byzantine emperor Basil I, who wouldn't call a Frank an emperor. Louis died in August 875 with only a daughter. The imperial crown was up for grabs.

claims.text: Louis was held prisoner by the prince of Benevento in 871.
claims.note: The Annals of St-Bertin and southern Italian chroniclers such as Erchempert report it.

claims.text: He wrote to Basil I defending his right to be called emperor.
claims.note: The letter survives, copied into the Salerno Chronicle; most scholars accept it, though some think it was polished by a papal secretary.

reigns.hook: No son, no clear heir. His uncles Charles the Bald and Louis the German both want the crown. Charles moves first, crossing the Alps fast, and the pope is waiting for him in Rome.

reigns.tagline: The baby of the family, emperor at last for two years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Uncle; son of Louis the Pious
reigns.previously: Louis II dies with no son. His uncles race for Italy.
paragraphs: Charles was the late baby whose birth had set his half-brothers against their father. As a young man he stood with his brother Louis at Strasbourg in 842 and swore the famous oaths against Lothair. At Verdun he won the western kingdom, and he spent the next thirty years holding it together against rebel nobles, Bretons and Vikings.

The Vikings sailed up the Seine almost at will. In 845 Charles paid them 7,000 pounds of silver to leave Paris. Later he built fortified bridges to block the rivers. When Louis II died he raced to Rome and was crowned emperor on Christmas Day 875, beating his brother Louis the German to it.

When Louis the German died in 876, Charles tried to grab his lands and was beaten at Andernach by his nephew. In 877 he went back to Italy to help the pope against Arab raiders, fell ill on the way home over the Alps and died on 6 October.

claims.text: 'The Bald' was a joke, because he was actually very hairy.
claims.note: The nickname is only recorded long after his death, and the ironic reading is a modern guess. Nobody knows what his hair was like.

claims.text: His Jewish doctor Zedekiah poisoned him.
claims.note: The Annals of St-Bertin and later chronicles repeat the rumour. It fits a nasty medieval stereotype and there's no evidence for it.

reigns.hook: The throne sits empty for over three years. The pope needs a protector against the raiders, and he's looking at the youngest son of Louis the German, a man called Charles.

reigns.tagline: He put Charlemagne's empire back together, then lost it
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew; son of Louis the German
reigns.previously: Charles the Bald dies crossing the Alps. The throne sits empty.
paragraphs: Charles had luck that looked like destiny. He became king of Italy, then emperor in 881. As his brothers died off, he inherited the whole eastern kingdom. In 884 the last adult king in the west died in a hunting accident and the western nobles invited Charles in too. For a few years, almost all of Charlemagne's empire had one ruler again.

Then came the Vikings. In 885 a huge fleet besieged Paris. Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin held out for months. In 886 Charles finally arrived with an army, and instead of fighting he paid the Vikings 700 pounds of silver and let them sail on to raid Burgundy. The Parisians were disgusted.

He was also ill, with headaches bad enough for surgeons to cut his scalp. In November 887 his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia marched on him and the eastern nobles dropped Charles. He died two months later, and the empire fell apart for good.

claims.text: He paid off the Vikings outside Paris rather than fight them.
claims.note: Abbo of Saint-Germain, a monk inside the besieged city, describes it in his poem on the siege, as do the Annals of St-Vaast.

claims.text: Nobody called him 'the Fat' while he was alive.
claims.note: The nickname first appears in chronicles a few centuries later.

claims.text: His own men strangled him after he was deposed.
claims.note: One version of the Annals of Fulda passes on the rumour. Other sources just say he fell ill and died.

reigns.hook: Charles is gone and nobody can hold the whole empire now. Kings spring up everywhere, Italian lords fight over the imperial crown, and in Rome a dead pope is about to be put on trial.

reigns.tagline: The bastard king who stormed Rome, then froze
reigns.previously: Charles the Fat is deposed by his nephew. He's dead within two months.
paragraphs: Arnulf was the son of King Carloman of Bavaria and a woman he never married, so he grew up a royal bastard ruling the frontier march of Carinthia. In November 887 he marched on his sick uncle, Charles the Fat. The eastern nobles switched sides at Tribur, and Arnulf was king of East Francia. Everywhere else, local strongmen crowned themselves: Odo in Paris, Rudolf in Burgundy, Guy and Berengar in Italy.

He was a fighter. In 891 he caught a Viking army on the river Dyle, near Leuven, and wiped it out. He spent years at war with Svatopluk of Moravia. Then Pope Formosus begged him to rescue Rome from the dukes of Spoleto. In February 896 his men stormed the city walls and Formosus crowned him emperor.

Weeks later, marching on Spoleto, Arnulf was struck down by a paralysing illness. He was carried home to Bavaria and never really ruled again. He died at Regensburg in December 899, leaving a six-year-old son.

claims.text: Lambert's mother Ageltrude poisoned Arnulf in 896.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, writing about 60 years later, blames her. Most historians think it was a stroke.

claims.text: At the end he was eaten alive by lice.
claims.note: Liutprand says no doctor could stop the tiny vermin. Writers used the same grisly death to shame other villains, so it may be invented.

claims.text: His army routed the Vikings on the Dyle in 891.
claims.note: The Annals of Fulda and Regino of Prüm both describe the battle and its aftermath.

reigns.hook: Arnulf won his crown in Rome, but he wasn't the first emperor of these years. Rewind to 891, when a duke from Spoleto talked a pope into crowning him in St Peter's.

reigns.tagline: The duke who grabbed the emperor's crown
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival of Arnulf; Duke of Spoleto
reigns.previously: Arnulf dies, paralysed. Now rewind to Italy, eight years earlier.
paragraphs: Guy ran the duchy of Spoleto in central Italy, a big, warlike family with Frankish roots and Carolingian kin. When Charles the Fat fell in 887 he aimed high. He even had himself crowned king of the West Franks at Langres, then saw he had no support there and turned back to Italy.

There he fought Berengar of Friuli for the Italian crown, won at the Trebbia in 889 and was crowned king at Pavia. On 21 February 891 Pope Stephen V crowned him emperor in Rome. The next pope, Formosus, had to crown Guy's son Lambert as co-emperor in 892, while secretly writing to Arnulf for help.

Arnulf came in 894, stormed Bergamo and hanged its count at the gate. Guy kept out of his way, and the Germans went home. Late that year, as he prepared for the next round, Guy died suddenly near the river Taro.

claims.text: Guy was crowned king of the West Franks at Langres in 888 before giving up.
claims.note: Frankish annals record the coronation by the bishop of Langres. Guy left when Odo of Paris won the nobles over.

claims.text: Pope Formosus secretly begged Arnulf to come and free Rome from Guy.
claims.note: The Annals of Fulda record envoys from Formosus reaching Arnulf and asking him to come to Italy.

reigns.hook: Guy is dead, and the imperial crown rests on the head of his son Lambert, a teenager. Behind the boy stands his ferocious mother, Ageltrude. She has a score to settle with the pope.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor and the pope on trial
reigns.cameToPower: Sole emperor on his father's death
reigns.previously: Guy dies suddenly. His teenage son is emperor on his own.
paragraphs: Lambert had been co-emperor since he was about 12. Now he had the job alone, with his mother Ageltrude at his side. In February 896 Arnulf's army stormed Rome and the pope crowned the German instead. Then Arnulf fell ill and went home, and the Spoletans came back.

In January 897 Pope Stephen VI, now on Lambert's side, had Formosus dug up. The rotting corpse was dressed in papal robes, put on trial and found guilty. Its blessing fingers were cut off and it was thrown in the Tiber. Rome rioted and Stephen was strangled in prison.

Lambert grew up fast. He split Italy with Berengar and made peace with Pope John IX, who scrapped the corpse trial and Arnulf's coronation. Then in October 1898 he fell from his horse hunting at Marengo and died, still under 20.

claims.text: A pope's corpse was put on trial in 897, the 'Cadaver Synod'.
claims.note: Auxilius and Eugenius Vulgarius wrote about it within a few years, and Pope John IX's synod of 898 annulled the verdict.

claims.text: Lambert and Ageltrude were behind the Cadaver Synod.
claims.note: They had the motive, since Formosus had crowned Arnulf. No source shows them giving the order.

claims.text: Lambert was murdered, his neck broken by a nobleman whose father he had executed.
claims.note: Liutprand tells this story. Other sources speak only of a fall while hunting.

reigns.hook: Lambert is dead and Italy falls to Berengar. North of the Alps, Arnulf dies the next year, leaving a six-year-old boy, a squabbling nobility and a kingdom wide open to Magyar raiders.

reigns.tagline: A six-year-old king, and the Magyars at the door
reigns.previously: Lambert dies in a hunting fall. In the east, Arnulf dies too.
paragraphs: Louis was raised king at Forchheim in February 900, aged six. A boy can't rule, so bishops did it for him: Archbishop Hatto of Mainz and Bishop Salomo of Constance signed the charters and steered the court. The great families fought each other, and the Conradines of Franconia won a bloody feud against the Babenbergs.

The real terror was the Magyars, horsemen from the Hungarian plain who struck fast and vanished. On 4 July 907 they destroyed a Bavarian army near Pressburg, killing its margrave and the archbishop of Salzburg. In 910 Louis led an army himself and was beaten near Augsburg.
He was sickly and never had children. In September 911 he died at about 18. He was the last Carolingian to rule east of the Rhine.

claims.text: Archbishop Hatto tricked Adalbert of Babenberg out of his castle with a false promise, and Adalbert was beheaded.
claims.note: Widukind of Corvey tells it 60 years later. Adalbert's execution in 906 is real. Hatto's trick may be storytelling.

claims.text: The Magyars wiped out the Bavarian army at Pressburg in 907.
claims.note: Several sets of annals list the dead, including Margrave Luitpold and Archbishop Theotmar of Salzburg.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 901. Another Carolingian Louis, a young king from Provence, has crossed the Alps to grab the emperor's crown. Waiting for him in Italy is Berengar, who hates to share.

reigns.tagline: Emperor for four years, blind for twenty-three
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival; grandson of Emperor Louis II
reigns.previously: Louis the Child dies at 18, the last Carolingian in the east.
paragraphs: Louis was the son of Boso, a count who made himself king of Provence in 879, and of Ermengard, daughter of Emperor Louis II. That gave him Carolingian blood and a claim on Italy. In 900 Italian nobles tired of Berengar invited him in. He was crowned king at Pavia, and in February 901 Pope Benedict IV made him emperor in Rome.

Berengar fought back and drove him out in 902, and Louis swore never to return. In 905 he came back anyway and took Verona. Berengar's supporters let their man into the city by night. Louis was caught, and on 21 July 905 he was blinded.
He went home to Provence and kept calling himself emperor for another 23 years. His cousin Hugh of Arles did the real work.

claims.text: Louis was blinded as the price of breaking his oath never to return to Italy.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, writing decades later, ties the blinding to the broken oath. The blinding itself is recorded in several sources.

claims.text: After the blinding, Hugh of Arles ran Provence in his name.
claims.note: Charters show Hugh as the leading man of the kingdom. He later became king of Italy himself.

reigns.hook: Back north, 911. The boy king Louis is dead and there are no Carolingian men left in the east. For the first time, the Frankish nobles will have to choose a king from outside the family.

reigns.tagline: The east's first non-Carolingian king, and his dukes said no
reigns.previously: Louis the Blind goes home to Provence, blind but still 'emperor'.
paragraphs: Conrad was a Conradine, the family that had just won the feud with the Babenbergs, and Duke of Franconia. On 10 November 911 the nobles met at Forchheim and made him king. It was a big moment: for the first time the eastern Franks chose a king with no Carolingian father. Lotharingia refused him and went over to the king of the West Franks. Conrad tried to win it back and failed.

Then the dukes turned on him. Henry of Saxony, Arnulf of Bavaria and two Swabian brothers, Erchanger and Berthold, all fought him. In 917 he had the Swabians beheaded. Meanwhile the Magyars rode in at will, as far as Basel.
Worn down, Conrad died on 23 December 918 and was buried at Fulda. His own family had failed. The next king would come from his fiercest enemy.

claims.text: On his deathbed Conrad told his brother Eberhard to take the royal insignia to Henry of Saxony.
claims.note: Widukind of Corvey tells the story about 50 years later. It flatters Henry's family, who were Widukind's patrons.

claims.text: Conrad died from a wound taken fighting the Bavarians.
claims.note: Some later accounts link his death to his Bavarian campaign. The annals just record that he died.

reigns.hook: Rewind to Rome, December 915. Berengar of Friuli, the old warhorse who has fought for Italy since 887, is about to get what he always wanted. The pope will crown him emperor.

reigns.tagline: Forty years fighting for Italy, and a knife at the end
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Rival; grandson of Louis the Pious
reigns.previously: Conrad I is dead, his kingdom in pieces. Italy has its own story.
paragraphs: Berengar's mother was a daughter of Louis the Pious, and he had been Margrave of Friuli in north-east Italy. He was crowned king of Italy in 887 and spent the next 30 years fighting for it: against Guy, against Lambert, against Louis of Provence, whom he had blinded. In 899 the Magyars crushed his army at the Brenta.

He survived everything. In December 915 Pope John X crowned him emperor in Rome, and a court poet wrote a Latin epic about his deeds. But the Italian nobles were sick of him. They brought in Rudolf II of Burgundy, who beat him at Fiorenzuola in 923.
Berengar fell back to Verona. On 7 April 924 one of his own followers stabbed him to death. Nobody was crowned emperor again for 38 years.

claims.text: He was murdered by Flambert, a man whose son he had stood godfather to.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona tells the story with a twist of betrayal. The murder is certain; the details are his.

claims.text: A poet wrote an epic, the Gesta Berengarii, to celebrate his coronation.
claims.note: The anonymous poem survives in a single manuscript, written in his lifetime.

claims.text: He hired Magyar raiders, who burned Pavia in 924.
claims.note: Liutprand blames Berengar's Magyar allies for the fire. How far Berengar controlled them is unclear.

reigns.hook: Italy now has no emperor at all. North of the Alps, the Franks and Saxons have already chosen a new king: the duke of Saxony. Legend says he was out catching birds when they found him.

reigns.tagline: The Saxon bird-catcher who built a kingdom
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Duke of Saxony; Conrad I's rival
reigns.previously: Conrad I is dead. In Italy, old Emperor Berengar clings on.
paragraphs: Henry was never emperor. He was king of East Francia, and he made a point of being modest about it. When the archbishop of Mainz offered to anoint him with holy oil, Henry said no thanks. Instead of fighting the great dukes of Bavaria and Swabia to the death, he made deals with them: keep your duchy, accept me as king.

His big problem was the Magyars, raiders from the Hungarian plain who had been burning their way across Germany for years. In 926 Henry captured one of their leaders and swapped him for a nine-year truce, paying tribute. He used the time to build fortified strongholds and train armoured cavalry. In 933, when the Magyars came back, he beat them at Riade.
He added Lotharingia to his kingdom too. Before he died of a stroke in 936, he made sure the crown would pass to one son, Otto, without carving the kingdom up.

claims.text: The messengers found Henry out catching birds when they came to tell him he was king.
claims.note: The story turns up only in later medieval writers, long after Henry died. It gave him his nickname.

claims.text: He refused to be anointed by the Church at his election.
claims.note: Widukind of Corvey reports his polite refusal. Historians argue about why.

reigns.hook: Henry is dead, and for once there's no carve-up. The kingdom goes whole to his son Otto, who means to be crowned in Charlemagne's own church at Aachen.

reigns.tagline: The king who stopped the Magyars and revived the empire
reigns.previously: Henry the Fowler dies at Memleben, his son Otto named as heir.
paragraphs: Otto was crowned at Aachen in August 936, sitting on Charlemagne's throne. His family didn't share his enthusiasm. His half-brother, his brother Henry and later his own son Liudolf all rebelled. He crushed them one by one. His first wife was Edith, an English princess. After she died he married Adelaide, the widowed queen of Italy, and claimed Italy as well.

On 10 August 955 the Magyars came back in force and besieged Augsburg. Otto met them on the Lechfeld and wiped out their army. The raids that had terrorised Germany for sixty years stopped for good. His men are said to have hailed him as emperor on the battlefield.

On 2 February 962 Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome. Many historians date the Holy Roman Empire from that day. Otto deposed the same pope a year later. He had his son Otto II crowned co-emperor and found him a Byzantine bride. He died in 973.

claims.text: He carried the Holy Lance, said to hold a nail from the Cross, at the Lechfeld.
claims.note: Widukind of Corvey mentions the lance. Whether it was really at the battle, and what it really is, are open questions.

claims.text: Pope John XII died in the bed of a married woman, struck by the Devil or her husband.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, Otto's man and the pope's enemy, tells the story. He was hardly neutral.

claims.text: Queen Edith's bones were found in Magdeburg Cathedral in 2008.
claims.note: Scientists identified the remains in her tomb and tests matched an Anglo-Saxon woman raised in southern England.

reigns.hook: Otto the Great is dead. His heir is a 17-year-old who has never had to fight for anything, married to a Byzantine princess the Germans aren't sure they want.

reigns.tagline: The young emperor who swam for his life
reigns.previously: Otto the Great dies at Memleben, 37 years after taking the throne.
paragraphs: In 972 Otto had married Theophanu, a Byzantine noblewoman sent from Constantinople. She was the emperor's niece, not a princess born in the purple as hoped, and some Germans grumbled. She turned out to be clever, tough and one of the most capable people at court.

Otto spent his early years putting down his cousin Henry the Wrangler, duke of Bavaria. In 978 King Lothair of France raided Aachen; Otto struck back with an army that reached the walls of Paris. Then he turned to southern Italy, wanting to throw out the Arab raiders. On 13 July 982 at Stilo, in Calabria, his army was cut to pieces. Otto barely escaped.

Worse followed. In 983 the Slavs east of the Elbe rose up and destroyed German churches and forts. At a meeting at Verona, Otto had his three-year-old son elected king. Then he caught a fever in Rome and died on 7 December 983, aged 28. He is the only emperor buried at St Peter's.

claims.text: After Stilo he escaped by swimming out to a Greek ship, then leapt overboard and swam to shore.
claims.note: Thietmar of Merseburg tells the story vividly. He was writing decades later, and the details sound polished.

claims.text: He made his final fever worse by swallowing a huge dose of aloes as medicine.
claims.note: Thietmar says so. Nobody can check it, but the medicine was a known purge.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and his heir is three years old. Before the little boy can even be crowned, Henry the Wrangler breaks out of prison and comes looking for him.

reigns.tagline: The boy emperor who dreamed of reviving Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Verona, crowned at Aachen
reigns.previously: Otto II dies of fever in Rome. His heir is three years old.
paragraphs: Otto was crowned at Aachen on Christmas Day 983. Weeks later his cousin Henry the Wrangler kidnapped him and tried to take the crown. The nobles wouldn't back Henry, and he had to hand the boy back to his mother. Theophanu ruled for her son until she died in 991, then his grandmother Adelaide took over.

Otto grew up clever and dreamy, brought up on Greek and Latin. In 996 he made his cousin Bruno pope and was crowned emperor by him. Then he put his brilliant tutor Gerbert on the papal throne as Sylvester II. Otto built a palace in Rome and spoke of 'renewing the empire of the Romans'. In 1000 he went on pilgrimage to Gniezno in Poland, then on to Aachen, where he opened Charlemagne's tomb.
The Romans weren't grateful. In 1001 they rose and chased him out of the city. He was waiting for troops to take it back when he died of fever in January 1002, aged 21, unmarried and childless.

claims.text: When Otto opened the tomb, he found Charlemagne sitting upright on a throne.
claims.note: Thietmar only says Otto opened the grave and took a cross. The seated Charlemagne comes from the Novalesa Chronicle, written decades later.

claims.text: A Byzantine princess was on her way to marry him when he died.
claims.note: Several chroniclers report that a bride from Constantinople had reached Italy; she sailed home.

claims.text: He was poisoned by Stephania, widow of a Roman rebel he had executed.
claims.note: This romantic revenge tale appears only in much later writers. Malaria is the likelier killer.

reigns.hook: Otto has no son. As his body is carried north over the Alps, his cousin Henry of Bavaria stops the funeral party. He wants the royal regalia, and the crown that goes with them.

reigns.tagline: The saint king who grabbed the crown on the road
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the regalia, crowned at Mainz
reigns.previously: Otto III dies at 21 in Italy, with no son and no obvious heir.
paragraphs: Henry was Duke of Bavaria and grandson of Otto the Great's brother. When Otto III's funeral party came north, Henry met it on the road and took the royal regalia for himself. Other princes wanted the crown too, but Henry moved fastest. He was crowned at Mainz in June 1002, then spent years riding round the kingdom to win over the doubters.

He fought on and off for fifteen years with Bolesław the Brave of Poland and was crowned emperor in Rome in 1014. His pet project was Bamberg, where in 1007 he founded a new bishopric and poured money into the cathedral. He and his wife Cunigunde had no children. The Church later made saints of them both, and stories grew up that they had lived as brother and sister.
Henry died in July 1024 and was buried in his beloved Bamberg. He was the last of the Ottonians. The family that had built the empire was gone, and the princes had to choose a new king from scratch.

claims.text: Cunigunde proved her innocence by walking barefoot over red-hot ploughshares.
claims.note: Told in saints' lives written long after her death, when the couple were being promoted for sainthood. Nothing from her lifetime mentions it.

claims.text: Henry and Cunigunde never slept together, by mutual vow.
claims.note: Their childlessness is certain. The vow of chastity appears in later saints' lives; modern historians think it was an explanation invented after the fact.

claims.text: Henry was canonised in 1146 and Cunigunde in 1200.
claims.note: Both canonisations are recorded in papal documents.

reigns.hook: The princes gather in a meadow on the Rhine. Two cousins, both named Conrad, are in the running. Only one will walk away a king.

reigns.tagline: A count from the Rhine who ended up with three crowns
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Distant kinsman; descended from Otto I
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Kamba on the Rhine
reigns.previously: Henry II dies childless. The Ottonian line is finished.
paragraphs: Conrad was no royal prince. He was a Frankish nobleman with good blood, a sharp mind and a clever wife, Gisela of Swabia. In September 1024 the princes met at Kamba on the Rhine and picked him over his younger cousin, also called Conrad. His chaplain Wipo wrote it all down, which is why we know so much about this king.

He was crowned emperor in Rome at Easter 1027, with King Cnut of England and Denmark watching. When the last king of Burgundy died in 1032, Conrad claimed his kingdom, which stretched from Basel to Provence. That made him king of Germany, Italy and Burgundy at once. He also began a huge new cathedral at Speyer as a family tomb.

Conrad died at Utrecht in June 1039 and was carried back to be buried at Speyer. He had planned ahead. His son Henry had been crowned king years earlier, so the crown passed over without any election fight. The new Salian dynasty was off to a strong start.

claims.text: A saying went round that Conrad's saddle carried Charlemagne's stirrups.
claims.note: Wipo records the proverb in his Deeds of Conrad, meaning Conrad was a worthy heir to Charlemagne.

claims.text: Cnut and Rudolf III of Burgundy walked beside him at his imperial coronation.
claims.note: Wipo describes both kings at the ceremony, and Cnut mentions the trip in a letter to the English.

claims.text: Conrad began Speyer Cathedral as his family's burial church.
claims.note: Building started around 1030. He, Gisela and later Salian kings are buried there.

reigns.hook: Conrad's son is just 22, already crowned and ready. He has a fierce sense of his duty to God, and he's about to sort out the popes himself.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who sacked three popes in one go
reigns.previously: Conrad II dies at Utrecht. His son is already a crowned king.
paragraphs: Henry was serious, pious and very sure of himself. He married Agnes of Poitou and preached peace across his lands, forgiving his own enemies in public to set an example. He also believed an emperor answered to God for the state of the Church, and the Church was in a mess.

By 1046 three men all claimed to be pope. Henry marched to Italy and held a synod at Sutri, where he had them removed. He then put a German bishop on the papal throne, who crowned him emperor on Christmas Day. Over the next ten years Henry chose pope after pope, including his reforming kinsman Leo IX. No emperor ever had more power over Rome.

The trouble was that the reformers he backed started to ask why an emperor should pick popes at all. Then in 1056 Henry fell ill and died in the Harz mountains, aged only 39. His heir was a little boy of five.

claims.text: At Sutri in 1046 Henry deposed rival popes Sylvester III and Gregory VI, and Benedict IX was deposed soon after in Rome.
claims.note: Recorded in several contemporary chronicles and papal lists. Exactly who was deposed where is still argued over in detail.

claims.text: He was called “the Black” because of his dark beard.
claims.note: The nickname appears only in later writers. The beard explanation is a guess.

claims.text: Gregory VI had bought the papacy from Benedict IX.
claims.note: Contemporaries accused him of it. Gregory may have paid Benedict to step aside in good faith.

reigns.hook: A five-year-old wears the crown, his mother runs the kingdom, and the reformers Henry helped are getting ideas. That boy will one day stand barefoot in the snow.

reigns.tagline: Barefoot in the snow, begging a pope's forgiveness
reigns.cameToPower: Inherited the crown as a small boy
reigns.reignEnded: Forced to abdicate by his own son
reigns.previously: Henry III dies at 39. His heir is a boy of five.
paragraphs: Henry grew up fast and angry. At eleven he was kidnapped on a boat by the Archbishop of Cologne, and he jumped into the Rhine to escape. As a young king he fought a bitter war with the Saxons. Then he clashed with Pope Gregory VII over who got to appoint bishops. In 1076 Henry told Gregory to step down. Gregory excommunicated him, and the German princes threatened to dump their king.

So in January 1077 Henry crossed the Alps in winter to the castle of Canossa, where the pope was staying. He stood outside as a penitent for three days until Gregory let him in and lifted the ban. It worked for a while. Later Henry took Rome, set up his own pope and was crowned emperor in 1084. Gregory died in exile.

His real enemies turned out to be his sons. His eldest rebelled in the 1090s. Then in 1105 his younger son Henry turned on him, lured him to a meeting and locked him up. On 31 December 1105 the old emperor was made to give up his crown. He escaped and died at Liège the next summer, still excommunicated.

claims.text: Henry stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa for three days.
claims.note: The three days are well attested. The bare feet and snow come mostly from Lambert of Hersfeld, who disliked Henry and loved a dramatic scene.

claims.text: Aged eleven, Henry leapt into the Rhine to escape his kidnappers at Kaiserswerth.
claims.note: Lambert of Hersfeld tells the story, and other sources confirm the kidnapping in 1062.

claims.text: His body lay unburied in an unconsecrated chapel at Speyer for five years.
claims.note: He died excommunicated. Chroniclers report he was only buried in the cathedral in 1111, once the ban was lifted.

reigns.hook: Rewind to March 1077. Henry has just been forgiven at Canossa, but the princes who wanted him gone have already picked a new king: his own brother-in-law, Rudolf of Swabia.

reigns.tagline: The rival king who lost his sword hand
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by rebel princes at Forchheim
reigns.reignEnded: Lost his hand and life on the Elster
reigns.previously: Henry IV dies deposed. Now, back to 1077 and his first rival.
paragraphs: Rudolf was Duke of Swabia and Henry IV's brother-in-law twice over: he married Henry's sister, and later the sister of Henry's queen. In 1075 he fought for Henry against the Saxons. Then the pope excommunicated the king, and Rudolf joined the princes who wanted him gone. On 15 March 1077, at Forchheim, they elected Rudolf instead. He was the first anti-king in the empire's history.

The timing was awkward, since Henry had just been forgiven at Canossa. Rudolf was crowned at Mainz on 25 May, but the townspeople rose against him and he fled to Saxony. The Saxons never fully trusted a southerner, and he had to buy loyalty with crown and Church lands. Henry stripped him of Swabia and gave it to Frederick of Staufen, whose family would one day rule the empire.

In March 1080 Pope Gregory VII finally backed Rudolf and excommunicated Henry again. That October the armies met on the White Elster. Rudolf's side won, but he lost his right hand and took a sword in the belly. He died the next day and was buried in Merseburg Cathedral. Without him the revolt lost its heart.

claims.text: Henry's side said that losing the hand he had sworn loyalty with was God's verdict on a traitor.
claims.note: Writers loyal to Henry made exactly this point soon after the battle. It was propaganda, but they really said it.

claims.text: Rudolf's mummified right hand is still kept at Merseburg.
claims.note: The cathedral has kept a mummified hand since the Middle Ages. That it is Rudolf's rests on tradition.

claims.text: His bronze grave slab is the oldest of its kind in central Europe.
claims.note: It was made soon after his death and still lies in Merseburg Cathedral, once covered in gilding and stones.

reigns.hook: Rudolf is dead, and Henry IV outlasts every rival the princes can find. In the end it takes his own son to bring him down, and that son now wears the crown.

reigns.tagline: He jailed his father, then the pope
reigns.previously: Henry IV outlives his rivals, only to be toppled by his own son.
paragraphs: Henry had sided with the Church to topple his father. Once in power, he wanted the same rights over bishops that his father had fought for. In 1111 he went to Rome to be crowned. When talks broke down he arrested Pope Paschal II and his cardinals, and kept them prisoner until the pope agreed to crown him and give way.

In 1114 he married Matilda, the twelve-year-old daughter of Henry I of England, who brought a huge dowry. The German princes kept rebelling, and he lost a battle to the Saxons at Welfesholz in 1115. At last, at Worms in 1122, emperor and pope did a deal. The Church would choose bishops, and the emperor could watch and hand over their lands.

That Concordat of Worms closed half a century of war with the papacy. Three years later Henry died at Utrecht with no children. Matilda went home to England. The Salian dynasty was over, and the princes were ready to choose for themselves.

claims.text: Henry held Pope Paschal II prisoner until he agreed to crown him.
claims.note: Described by chroniclers on both sides in 1111. Paschal later took back the rights he had granted.

claims.text: Matilda kept the title “Empress” for the rest of her life, even after remarrying.
claims.note: Her charters and English chroniclers use it. She fought Stephen for the English throne as “the Empress”.

claims.text: On his deathbed Henry left the imperial regalia in Matilda's keeping.
claims.note: Chroniclers say she held them after his death, but accounts differ on his wishes. The Archbishop of Mainz soon got them back for the election.

reigns.hook: Henry's nephew, Frederick of Swabia, thinks the crown is his. The princes have other ideas, and an old enemy from Saxony is waiting.

reigns.tagline: The princes' pick, chosen to keep the Staufer out
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Mainz over a Staufer
reigns.previously: Henry V dies childless. The Salians are gone.
paragraphs: Lothair was Duke of Saxony and had beaten Henry V in battle. When the princes met at Mainz in 1125, everyone expected Henry's nephew Frederick of Swabia to win. But the Archbishop of Mainz worked the room, and the princes chose the Saxon instead. Frederick's family, the Staufer, were furious.

Lothair married his only daughter Gertrude to Henry the Proud, head of the Welf family. That made the Welfs his allies and the Staufer his enemies. The Staufer even set up Frederick's brother Conrad as a rival king. Lothair wore them down, and in 1133 Pope Innocent II crowned him emperor in Rome.

He went back to Italy to fight the Normans in the south. On the way home in December 1137 he died in a peasant's hut in Tyrol. He had already handed the royal insignia to his son-in-law Henry the Proud. Everyone assumed the Welf would be next.

claims.text: Lothair died in a peasant's hut at Breitenwang.
claims.note: Reported by chroniclers of the time. He was buried at Königslutter, the abbey he had founded.

claims.text: The 1125 election was the first truly free choice of a German king.
claims.note: Later writers saw it that way. Historians point out that the Archbishop of Mainz steered it hard.

claims.text: He gave Henry the Proud the royal insignia on his deathbed.
claims.note: Otto of Freising and other chroniclers say Henry held the regalia after Lothair's death.

reigns.hook: Henry the Proud holds the crown jewels and thinks the throne is his. But the princes fear him. A quick, quiet election is being planned behind his back.

reigns.tagline: The first Staufer king, and a crusade gone wrong
reigns.previously: Lothair III dies in Tyrol. His Welf son-in-law holds the regalia.
paragraphs: Conrad was the grandson of Henry IV and the man Lothair had beaten. In March 1138 a small group of princes met at Koblenz and quickly elected him before Henry the Proud could act. Conrad then stripped Henry of his duchies of Bavaria and Saxony. That started a feud between Welf and Staufer that would run for a hundred years.

In 1147 he went on the Second Crusade. His army was cut to pieces by the Turks in Anatolia, and he fell ill. The siege of Damascus in 1148 failed after a few days. Conrad came home with nothing to show for it. He was never crowned emperor, which makes him a rare German king who never wore the imperial crown.

Dying at Bamberg in 1152, he passed over his own small son. He told the princes to choose his nephew Frederick instead, a grown man with a Welf mother and a Staufer father. He might be the one to end the feud.

claims.text: At Weinsberg in 1140 Conrad let the women leave with what they could carry, and they carried out their husbands.
claims.note: First told in the Royal Chronicle of Cologne. It's a famous story, but it can't be confirmed, and similar tales are told of other sieges.

claims.text: The battle cries “Welf!” and “Waiblingen!” were first heard at Weinsberg.
claims.note: Later writers say so. The names became the Guelfs and Ghibellines of Italian politics.

claims.text: Conrad was never crowned emperor.
claims.note: He planned a trip to Rome but died before he could go.

reigns.tagline: Red beard, big dreams, and a fatal river crossing
reigns.previously: Conrad III dies, passing over his own son for his nephew.
paragraphs: The Italians called him Barbarossa, Redbeard. Frederick was charming, tireless and set on making the empire great again. He gave his Welf cousin Henry the Lion a free hand in Saxony and Bavaria, and turned to Italy. He was crowned emperor in 1155, and in 1162 he flattened Milan for defying him.

The northern Italian cities banded together in the Lombard League and beat him at Legnano in 1176. Henry the Lion had refused to send help. A year later at Venice Frederick made peace with Pope Alexander III, whom he had fought for nearly twenty years, and bowed to kiss his feet. Back in Germany he took revenge, and Henry the Lion lost his duchies and went into exile.

In 1189, aged nearly seventy, Frederick led a huge army off on the Third Crusade. He beat the Turks at Iconium. Then on 10 June 1190 he drowned in the river Saleph in southern Anatolia. Without him, most of his army fell apart. His son Henry had been crowned king long before.

claims.text: Barbarossa is asleep inside the Kyffhäuser mountain, waiting to return when Germany needs him.
claims.note: The sleeping-emperor legend was first told of Frederick II and only later attached to Barbarossa.

claims.text: He knelt and kissed Pope Alexander III's feet at Venice in 1177.
claims.note: Several eyewitness chroniclers describe the scene in front of St Mark's.

claims.text: He drowned trying to cool off with a swim.
claims.note: Sources disagree. Some say he was swimming, others that he was thrown from his horse while crossing.

reigns.hook: Barbarossa's son is clever, cold and very ambitious. His wife is the heiress to Sicily, and soon the English king will fall into his hands.

reigns.tagline: He held Richard the Lionheart for ransom
reigns.previously: Barbarossa drowns on crusade. His son is already king.
paragraphs: Henry was as hard as his father was charming. He had married Constance, aunt and heir of the King of Sicily. When the king died in 1189, the Sicilians crowned someone else. Henry was crowned emperor in Rome in 1191, then besieged Naples and failed.

Then luck came his way. Richard the Lionheart, heading home from crusade, was captured near Vienna by Duke Leopold of Austria and handed over to Henry. The emperor held him for over a year and set a ransom of 150,000 marks. That silver paid for a new campaign, and at Christmas 1194 Henry was crowned King of Sicily in Palermo. The day after, Constance gave birth to their son Frederick.

Henry crushed Sicilian plots with savage punishments and tried to make the crown of Germany hereditary. The princes said no. He was planning a crusade when he died of fever at Messina in 1197, still in his early thirties. His son was not yet three.

claims.text: Constance gave birth to Frederick in a tent in the town square of Jesi, so nobody could doubt the baby was hers.
claims.note: She was 40 and had been childless for years. The public birth story comes from later chroniclers.

claims.text: Richard's ransom was 150,000 marks of silver.
claims.note: English chroniclers such as Roger of Howden give the figure. Not all of it was ever paid.

claims.text: Henry was the “Emperor Henry” whose love songs appear in the Codex Manesse.
claims.note: The songbook names a Kaiser Heinrich, and most scholars think it is Henry VI, but there is no proof.

reigns.hook: The emperor is dead and his heir is a toddler in Sicily. The German princes want a grown man, but they can't agree on which one. Soon there will be two kings.

reigns.tagline: One crown, two kings, and a murder at a wedding
reigns.previously: Henry VI dies of fever. His heir is a toddler in Sicily.
paragraphs: Philip was Barbarossa's youngest son. He had been trained for the Church, then made Duke of Swabia. With his nephew Frederick too young, the Staufer supporters elected Philip king in March 1198. Three months later the Welf party chose Otto of Brunswick. Germany now had two kings, and a long civil war began.

Philip held the real crown jewels but was crowned in the wrong place. Otto was crowned in the right place, Aachen, with copies. Pope Innocent III backed Otto. But princes kept changing sides, and by 1207 Philip was winning. Otto was penned up in his Brunswick lands, and the pope was ready to talk.

Then in June 1208 Philip went to his niece's wedding at Bamberg. During a break, Count Palatine Otto of Wittelsbach walked into his room and killed him with a sword. Philip was the first German king to be murdered. His rival suddenly had no one left to fight.

claims.text: Philip was the first German king to be murdered.
claims.note: No earlier king of the Germans had been assassinated. Chroniclers across Europe reported the killing.

claims.text: Otto of Wittelsbach killed him because Philip had broken off Otto's engagement to his daughter.
claims.note: This is the motive the chroniclers give. Some historians suspect a wider plot, but nobody has proved one.

claims.text: Philip was crowned with the genuine regalia, Otto with copies.
claims.note: Contemporaries argued over which mattered more: the right crown or the right place.

reigns.hook: Philip is dead and the princes switch sides overnight. Otto has the throne to himself at last. If only he could resist Sicily.

paragraphs: Otto was the son of Henry the Lion and grew up partly at the court of his uncle, Richard the Lionheart. Richard's money and the Archbishop of Cologne got him elected in 1198 as rival to Philip of Swabia. For ten years he was losing. Then Philip was murdered in 1208, and the princes accepted Otto as sole king.

Pope Innocent III crowned him emperor in Rome in 1209. Otto had promised to leave southern Italy alone, but within a year he invaded the Kingdom of Sicily, which belonged to the pope's ward, the young Frederick. Innocent excommunicated him. Many German princes deserted Otto and invited Frederick to come north.

Otto bet everything on an alliance with his other uncle, King John of England, against France. At Bouvines on 27 July 1214, Philip Augustus smashed their army. Otto fled the field, and his supporters melted away. He spent his last years in his family lands around Brunswick and died at the Harzburg in 1218.

claims.text: At Bouvines the French captured Otto's eagle standard, and Philip Augustus sent the eagle to Frederick II.
claims.note: French chronicler William the Breton, who was there, describes it.

claims.text: Otto was the only Welf ever to be emperor.
claims.note: No other member of the house held the imperial title.

claims.text: Richard the Lionheart bribed the electors to choose Otto.
claims.note: English money certainly backed Otto's campaign. How much went straight to electors is unclear.

reigns.hook: A boy from Sicily has crossed the Alps with almost no army. The German princes are flocking to him. They call him the child of Apulia.

reigns.tagline: The wonder of the world, at war with the popes
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned at Mainz as a rival king
reigns.previously: Otto IV invades Sicily, and the pope turns against him.
paragraphs: Frederick grew up an orphan in Palermo, a city of Greeks, Arabs, Jews and Latins. He spoke several languages and was curious about everything. In 1212, aged 17, he slipped across the Alps and won over the German princes. After Bouvines, Otto was finished. Frederick was crowned emperor in Rome in 1220.

He promised to go on crusade, then kept putting it off. In 1227 Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him. Frederick went anyway, and in 1229 he got Jerusalem back by treaty with the Sultan of Egypt, without a battle. He founded the University of Naples, wrote a famous book on falconry and kept a zoo with an elephant. Matthew Paris called him the wonder of the world.

The popes saw him as a monster. He was excommunicated again in 1239 and declared deposed in 1245. His eldest son Henry rebelled and died a prisoner. The wars with the papacy and the Lombard cities dragged on until Frederick died in Apulia in December 1250. His son Conrad inherited the fight.

claims.text: Frederick had babies raised in silence to discover humanity's original language. They all died.
claims.note: Told by the friar Salimbene, who hated Frederick and listed it among his “follies”.

claims.text: He wrote the falconry book The Art of Hunting with Birds.
claims.note: Copies survive, including one made for his son Manfred, with Frederick named as the author.

claims.text: He got Jerusalem back by treaty in 1229 while excommunicated.
claims.note: The treaty with Sultan al-Kamil is well documented. The pope had him banned for the whole trip.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1220. Before heading back to Italy, Frederick left Germany to his small son Henry. The boy would grow up, rule for himself and then turn on his father.

reigns.previously: Frederick II dies in 1250. Rewind thirty years, to his eldest son.
paragraphs: Frederick II's eldest son was born in Sicily in 1211 and crowned King of Sicily as a baby. In April 1220 his father had the German princes elect the boy King of the Romans, so that Germany would have a king while Frederick lived in Italy. Archbishop Engelbert of Cologne crowned him at Aachen on 8 May 1222 and ran the kingdom for him.

Henry grew up with poets at his court and a wife seven years older than him, Margaret of Austria. From 1228 he ruled for himself and sided with the towns against the princes. The princes complained to Frederick, who made Henry sign a charter in their favour at Worms in 1231 and swear obedience at Cividale in 1232. In 1234 the pope excommunicated him for getting in the inquisitors' way.

That autumn Henry rose in open revolt. When Frederick came north in 1235, the rebels melted away. Henry submitted at Wimpfen on 2 July and was deposed at Worms two days later, and his young brother Conrad took his place. Henry spent nearly seven years as a prisoner and died in Calabria in February 1242 after a fall from his horse.

claims.text: Henry had leprosy in his last years.
claims.note: A study of his skeleton in 1998–99 by Gino Fornaciari's team found advanced leprosy. It may explain why he was never released.

claims.text: His fatal fall was a deliberate attempt to kill himself.
claims.note: Some chroniclers say so. Others record it as an accident, and there is no way to check.

claims.text: He is numbered Henry (VII), in brackets, because he never ruled alone.
claims.note: Historians use the brackets so he does not clash with the Luxembourg emperor Henry VII, who ruled from 1308.

reigns.hook: Conrad, the younger brother, takes Henry's place. Ten years later the pope declares Frederick deposed, and the bishops go looking for a German prince willing to wear a rival crown.

reigns.tagline: The priests' king who won one battle
reigns.previously: Henry (VII) is deposed by his father and dies a prisoner.
paragraphs: Henry Raspe was Landgrave of Thuringia. He took over when his elder brother died on the way to a crusade, pushing his small nephew aside. For years he was loyal to the Staufer, and in 1242 Frederick II made him one of the men running Germany for the young Conrad IV.

In 1245 the pope declared Frederick deposed, and Raspe switched sides. On 22 May 1246 a group of mostly church princes elected him king. Papal money did much of the persuading, so his enemies called him the priests' king. In August he beat Conrad in battle on the Nidda, near Frankfurt.

That winter he went after the Staufer towns of Swabia and besieged Ulm and Reutlingen. Wounded in a skirmish at Reutlingen, he gave up the campaign and went home to the Wartburg, where he died on 16 February 1247. None of his three marriages had produced a child, and the old line of Thuringian landgraves ended with him.

claims.text: His enemies nicknamed him the priests' king (rex clericorum).
claims.note: The nickname appears soon after his election. Recent historians think it undersells him.

claims.text: He threw his widowed sister-in-law, St Elisabeth of Hungary, out of the Wartburg.
claims.note: Later saints' lives tell it that way. Historians think she more likely left by choice, to live in poverty as she had vowed.

claims.text: He won at the Nidda because Swabian lords deserted Conrad for papal money.
claims.note: Chroniclers blame a bought defection, but the accounts differ on who was paid and how much.

reigns.hook: Raspe is dead within a year. The pope's party will soon find another rival, but the Staufer still hold the south, and when Frederick dies in 1250 everything passes to his son Conrad.

paragraphs: Conrad's mother was Queen of Jerusalem and died soon after he was born, so he was a king from the cradle. He was elected King of the Romans in 1237. While Frederick fought in Italy, Conrad held Germany against two rival kings the pope had found, Henry Raspe and William of Holland.

After his father died Conrad went south to claim Sicily. His half-brother Manfred had kept it for him, and in 1253 Conrad took Naples. Pope Innocent IV excommunicated him and went shopping across Europe for a new king of Sicily. Conrad was never crowned emperor.

In May 1254 he died of fever at Lavello, aged 26. His son Conradin was two, back in Bavaria. In 1268 the boy came south to fight for his inheritance. Charles of Anjou beat him and had him beheaded in Naples. The Staufer were wiped out.

claims.text: Manfred poisoned Conrad.
claims.note: Rumours flew at the time, spread by the papal side. There's no evidence, and fever was common in that region.

claims.text: Conradin was beheaded in the market square of Naples in 1268, aged 16.
claims.note: Many chroniclers report the execution on Charles of Anjou's orders.

claims.text: Conrad was crowned King of Jerusalem.
claims.note: He held the title from birth but never went there to be crowned.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1247. With Raspe dead, the pope's party needs a new king. They pick William, the 20-year-old Count of Holland, and he will outlast every Staufer in Germany.

paragraphs: William became Count of Holland at seven, after his father was killed at a tournament. In 1247, aged 20, he was picked by the Rhineland archbishops as anti-king against the Staufer, with the pope's money behind him. He had to besiege Aachen for months before he could be crowned there, on 1 November 1248.
When Conrad IV died in 1254, William was the only king left. More princes accepted him, and he backed the new Rhenish League, a union of cities trying to keep the peace when nobody else would.
He spent his last years at war at home with the West Frisians. In January 1256, near Hoogwoud, his horse broke through the ice. Frisians caught him, still in armour, and killed him. He was 28.

claims.text: His son Floris V found his hidden body in 1282 and buried it at Middelburg.
claims.note: Melis Stoke and other Dutch chronicles, written decades later, say the Frisians had hidden it under a house floor.

claims.text: The Frisians didn't know they had killed a king until afterwards.
claims.note: Later chronicles say they only recognised him by his arms. It may be true, but it is a tidy story.

reigns.hook: A year with no king, and the electors smell money. Two rich foreigners want the crown. The first is the King of England's brother, and he's bringing chests of silver.

paragraphs: Richard was the younger son of King John and the brother of Henry III. Cornish tin made him one of the richest men in Europe. He had been on crusade, and his sister had married Frederick II. In January 1257 the archbishops of Cologne and Mainz and the Count Palatine elected him king, after he paid them enormous sums.
He was crowned at Aachen on 17 May 1257, but he made only four trips to Germany. The Rhineland accepted him; most of the empire carried on without him.

Back in England the barons rebelled. In 1264 Richard was captured at Lewes, hiding in a windmill. In 1271 his son Henry was murdered at Mass in Viterbo by the sons of Simon de Montfort. The next year Richard had a stroke and died at Berkhamsted.

claims.text: Richard bought his election with huge bribes to the electors.
claims.note: English chroniclers, Matthew Paris among them, were shocked by the sums he spent.

claims.text: After losing at Lewes he hid in a windmill and was mocked for it.
claims.note: The chroniclers report it, and the rebels' satirical Song against the King of Almaigne made fun of him.

reigns.hook: Rewind to April 1257. Richard isn't the only king elected that year. The other electors have chosen a man who will never set foot in Germany: the scholar King of Castile.

paragraphs: Alfonso was King of Castile and León, and through his mother a grandson of the Staufer king Philip of Swabia. In 1256 envoys from Pisa offered him the empire. On 1 April 1257 the archbishop of Trier, the Duke of Saxony and the Margrave of Brandenburg elected him, and Bohemia backed him too.

He never went to Germany. He poured Castile's money into what the Spanish called the 'business of the empire', lobbying popes who kept putting him off. At home he was a giant: laws, astronomy tables, songs to the Virgin and a book of chess and dice.
When Richard died, Alfonso pushed his claim again. The electors chose Rudolf of Habsburg instead. He went on protesting until 1275, when he met Pope Gregory X at Beaucaire and gave it up.

claims.text: He renounced his claim to the empire after meeting Pope Gregory X at Beaucaire in 1275.
claims.note: Papal letters and Castilian chronicles record the meeting and its outcome.

claims.text: He said that if he had been present at the Creation, he would have given God some useful advice.
claims.note: The quip is pinned on him by later writers, inspired by his astronomy. No source from his time records it.

reigns.hook: October 1273, Frankfurt. The electors pass over the mighty King of Bohemia and pick a 55-year-old Swabian count. His family name comes from a little castle in Switzerland: Habsburg.

reigns.tagline: The cheap count who founded a 600-year dynasty
reigns.previously: Richard is dead and Alfonso far away. The electors want a real king.
paragraphs: Rudolf was a tough, frugal count with lands in Swabia and Alsace. He was elected on 1 October 1273 and crowned at Aachen weeks later. His first job was getting back the crown lands and rights the princes had pocketed during the interregnum, and he went at it with lawsuits and sieges.

The big problem was Ottokar II of Bohemia, the richest prince in the empire, who refused to accept him and held Austria and Styria. Rudolf took them off him in 1276. Ottokar came back for revenge, and on 26 August 1278 he was beaten and killed at the Marchfeld. Rudolf handed Austria to his sons. That one move made the Habsburgs an Austrian family for the next 640 years.

He never got to Rome to be crowned emperor, and he failed to have his son Albert chosen as the next king. Feeling death coming, the old man rode to Speyer, where earlier kings lay buried, and died there in July 1291.

claims.text: When the sceptre was missing for the princes' oath, Rudolf grabbed a crucifix and used that instead.
claims.note: A popular story told in later chronicles and retold by Schiller. It fits his image as a pious, practical man, but no record of the day confirms it.

claims.text: Dying, he rode to Speyer to be buried among the old kings.
claims.note: The Styrian Rhyming Chronicle describes the journey, and he was buried in Speyer Cathedral, where his tomb slab survives.

reigns.hook: Rudolf wanted his son Albert to follow him. The electors have other ideas. They don't want a strong Habsburg dynasty, so they pick a poor count from Nassau they think they can control.

paragraphs: Adolf was a minor count from Nassau with little land and less money. The electors, led by the Archbishop of Mainz, chose him in May 1292 because he was cheap to control. He had to promise them castles, cash and favours before they'd vote.

Then he tried to build a power base of his own. In 1294 he signed up with Edward I of England against France and took English silver for it. He used money like that to buy Thuringia and Meissen and fought brutal campaigns to take them. The princes who'd made him were alarmed, and Albert of Habsburg was still waiting.
In June 1298 the electors met at Mainz, declared Adolf deposed and chose Albert. Adolf refused to go quietly. On 2 July the two armies met at Göllheim, and Adolf was killed in the fighting.

claims.text: Adolf hired himself out to Edward I of England.
claims.note: The 1294 alliance and Edward's payments are in the English records. Critics at home called him a mercenary king.

claims.text: Albert killed Adolf with his own hands at Göllheim.
claims.note: Some chroniclers say so, others name different knights. In the confusion of the battle nobody can be sure.

claims.text: Henry VII later had Adolf reburied in Speyer Cathedral, next to his rival Albert.
claims.note: Both kings were moved to Speyer in 1309, and memorials there still mark them.

reigns.hook: Adolf has been sacked, but he still has an army. Albert of Habsburg has the electors and an army too. Only one of them will ride away from Göllheim.

reigns.tagline: The one-eyed king killed by the nephew he cheated
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Rudolf I; Adolf's killer
reigns.previously: The electors sack Adolf. Albert of Habsburg is ready to fight for it.
paragraphs: Albert got the crown his father had wanted for him, but he had to kill a king to keep it. After Göllheim he was crowned at Aachen in August 1298. He was hard, stingy and blunt, and he had lost an eye a few years earlier after a mystery illness. People found him frightening.

He turned on the Rhineland electors who'd made him, broke their grip on the river tolls in 1301 and 1302, and made peace with Pope Boniface VIII. He tried to grab Bohemia for his son Rudolf when the old royal line died out in 1306, but the young man died the next year.

His nephew John kept asking for his share of the family lands and kept getting nothing. On 1 May 1308, as Albert rode home near the River Reuss, John and a few friends cut him down. Germany had lost its second king in ten years to violence.

claims.text: Doctors hung Albert upside down to drain out poison, and he lost an eye.
claims.note: Chroniclers tell this about his illness in 1295. He did lose an eye, but the cure story may be decoration.

claims.text: William Tell shot the apple off his son's head during Albert's reign.
claims.note: Later Swiss chronicles set the Tell story in these years. No document from the time mentions Tell at all.

reigns.hook: Albert's body lies by the river. The electors are in no hurry to crown another Habsburg. The Archbishop of Trier has a brother, a French-speaking count from Luxembourg.

reigns.tagline: Dante's dream emperor, killed by an Italian fever
reigns.previously: King Albert is murdered by his own nephew by the River Reuss.
paragraphs: Henry was a count of Luxembourg who grew up speaking French. His brother Baldwin was Archbishop of Trier, and that vote helped get him elected in November 1308. He married his son John to the heiress of Bohemia, and so a small family suddenly owned a kingdom.

Henry wanted what no king had managed since Frederick II: to go to Rome and be crowned emperor. He crossed the Alps in 1310, hoping to make peace among the Italian cities. Dante hailed him as a saviour. Instead the cities split for and against him and he spent his time besieging them.

On 29 June 1312 he was crowned emperor in Rome, with his enemies holding St Peter's, so the ceremony happened at the Lateran. He failed to take Florence. In August 1313 he died of malaria at Buonconvento, near Siena.

claims.text: Henry was poisoned by a Dominican friar in the communion wine.
claims.note: The rumour spread fast after his death and caused attacks on Dominicans, but the symptoms fit malaria.

claims.text: Dante saved a seat for Henry in Paradise.
claims.note: In Paradiso canto 30 Beatrice points out an empty throne waiting for "alto Arrigo", high Henry.

reigns.hook: Henry is dead in Tuscany, and the electors can't agree. In October 1314 they do something ridiculous: they elect two kings in two days, a Wittelsbach and a Habsburg.

reigns.tagline: The excommunicated emperor crowned by the people of Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Won half of a double election
reigns.previously: Henry VII dies of fever in Italy. The throne is empty again.
paragraphs: Louis, Duke of Upper Bavaria, was elected on 20 October 1314, one day after his cousin Frederick of Habsburg was elected by the other side. Both were crowned on the same day. Eight years of war followed, until Louis beat and captured Frederick at Mühldorf in 1322.

Then the pope weighed in. John XXII said no king could rule without his approval and excommunicated Louis in 1324, calling him simply "the Bavarian". Louis answered by marching on Rome, where in January 1328 a nobleman acting for the Roman people put the imperial crown on his head. He even set up his own pope.

In 1338 the electors declared that whoever they chose was king, pope or no pope. Louis piled up land for his sons: Brandenburg, Tyrol, Holland. That greed turned the princes against him, and in 1346 they elected a rival. A year later Louis collapsed and died while hunting a bear.

claims.text: His nickname "the Bavarian" started as a papal insult.
claims.note: John XXII refused to call him king and wrote of him as Ludovicus Bavarus. The name stuck.

claims.text: The thinkers William of Ockham and Marsilius of Padua fled to his court and wrote in his defence.
claims.note: Both were at his court in Munich and argued against papal power over emperors.

claims.text: He was poisoned, not felled by a stroke.
claims.note: Some contemporaries hinted at poison, but a sudden collapse during a hard hunt at 65 needs no plot.

reigns.hook: Rewind to October 1314. Louis wasn't the only king elected that week. His rival, Frederick of Habsburg, had been chosen the day before, and he would keep his word in a way nobody expected.

reigns.tagline: The rival king who went back to prison to keep his word
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Albert I; rival of Louis
reigns.previously: Louis the Bavarian dies on a bear hunt. Now, back to his old rival.
paragraphs: Frederick was Albert I's son, handsome and gracious, hence "the Fair". On 19 October 1314 the electors who didn't want Louis chose him. He was crowned at Bonn by the right archbishop in the wrong city, while Louis was crowned at Aachen by the wrong archbishop in the right one.

For eight years the cousins fought. On 28 September 1322 at Mühldorf, Frederick was captured and locked up in Trausnitz Castle. In 1325 Louis let him go home to talk his brothers into peace. They refused. So Frederick went back to captivity, as he'd promised.

Louis was so moved that he made Frederick a sort of co-king. It didn't amount to much. Frederick's warlike brother Leopold died in 1326, and Frederick, ill and worn out, retired to Austria and died in January 1330.

claims.text: Frederick returned to prison of his own free will to keep his word.
claims.note: Chroniclers of the time report it, and Schiller made it famous in his poem Deutsche Treue.

claims.text: Louis and Frederick shared a table and a bed as friends afterwards.
claims.note: Chroniclers say so. Sharing a bed was a public sign of trust then, so the story may be about politics as much as friendship.

reigns.hook: Frederick is gone, and Louis rules alone. But the pope still hates him, and in 1346 the electors find a rival with real power behind him: the grandson of Henry VII.

reigns.tagline: The scholar king who made Prague the heart of the empire
reigns.previously: Frederick the Fair dies. Louis rules on, still excommunicated.
paragraphs: He was christened Wenceslas but grew up at the French court and took the name Charles. Backed by the pope, who had once been his tutor, five electors chose him in July 1346 while Louis was still alive. A month later he fought at Crécy, where his blind father died charging the English. Charles was wounded and got away. Louis's death in 1347 saved him a war.

Charles preferred deals to battles. He was crowned emperor in Rome in 1355, then went home quickly. In 1356 he issued the Golden Bull, which fixed the seven electors and the rules for voting by majority. It stayed the empire's basic law until 1806.

His real love was Prague. He founded the first university in central Europe there in 1348, built a whole New Town and started the stone bridge that now bears his name. Before he died in 1378 he had his son Wenceslaus elected to follow him.

claims.text: The Charles Bridge foundation stone was laid at 5:31 on 9 July 1357, so the date reads 1-3-5-7-9-7-5-3-1.
claims.note: A neat palindrome, but the exact minute comes from much later writers. The year 1357 is right.

claims.text: Charles wrote his own autobiography.
claims.note: His Vita Caroli covers his early life, written in Latin. Few medieval kings did that.

claims.text: He paid the electors to choose his son.
claims.note: Charles promised huge sums and pledged imperial towns to get Wenceslaus elected in 1376.

reigns.hook: Charles leaves his son an empire in good order, a golden Prague and a schism that has just split the Church between two popes. Wenceslaus is 17. He'd rather go hunting.

reigns.tagline: The drunk king who lost Germany and barely noticed
reigns.previously: Charles IV dies in Prague. His son was elected two years earlier.
paragraphs: Wenceslaus started with every advantage and wasted them. He stayed in Bohemia, rarely went to Germany and never made it to Rome to be crowned emperor. His Bohemian nobles grew so fed up that they locked him up in 1394, and later his own brother Sigismund did the same.

He feuded with the Archbishop of Prague. In 1393 the archbishop's deputy, John of Nepomuk, was tortured and his body thrown off the Prague bridge into the river. Stories of the king's temper and drinking spread.

In August 1400 four Rhineland electors met at Lahnstein and declared him deposed as useless. Wenceslaus ignored them and stayed King of Bohemia. He lived to see the first Prague defenestration in 1419 and died a few weeks later, with Bohemia on the brink of revolution.

claims.text: John of Nepomuk was killed for refusing to tell the king what the queen had said in confession.
claims.note: This story appears decades after the event. The records point to a church quarrel between the king and the archbishop. Nepomuk was made a saint in 1729.

claims.text: Wenceslaus had a cook roasted on a spit for burning his dinner.
claims.note: A tale from hostile later writers. There's no reliable source for it.

claims.text: Being deposed in Germany made no difference to him in Bohemia.
claims.note: The Rhine electors had no say over Bohemia, and he stayed its king until he died in 1419.

reigns.hook: The electors have sacked a king. Now they need one who'll actually turn up. They pick one of their own, the Elector Palatine. Aachen slams its gates in his face.

reigns.tagline: The elector who got the crown and none of the power
reigns.previously: The electors depose Wenceslaus. He shrugs and stays in Prague.
paragraphs: Rupert was Elector Palatine, ruling from Heidelberg, and he was elected the day after Wenceslaus was dumped. He was serious and well meaning, but most of the empire didn't care. Aachen refused to let him in, so he was crowned at Cologne in January 1401.

He tried to win prestige the old way, by marching on Italy for an imperial crown. In autumn 1401 his army was beaten near Brescia by the Duke of Milan's troops, and he ran out of money and went home in 1402.

Back in Germany the princes and cities formed leagues against him. He spent his last years just holding on, then died in May 1410 at Landskron, near Oppenheim. He is buried in Heidelberg's Church of the Holy Spirit.

claims.text: Aachen, the traditional coronation city, shut its gates on Rupert.
claims.note: The city stayed loyal to Wenceslaus, so Rupert was crowned in Cologne instead.

claims.text: Rupert is the only German king buried in Heidelberg.
claims.note: His tomb, shared with his wife Elisabeth, is in the choir of the Church of the Holy Spirit.

reigns.hook: Rupert is dead, and the electors split again. Soon there are three kings, just as there are three popes. Someone has to clean up the mess, and Wenceslaus's ambitious brother wants the job.

reigns.tagline: He fixed the papacy and set Bohemia on fire
reigns.previously: Rupert dies at Landskron. The electors can't agree on anyone.
paragraphs: Sigismund was already King of Hungary, a vain, clever, charming man who spoke several languages. In 1410 rival electors chose him and his cousin Jobst, while his brother Wenceslaus still claimed the title. Jobst died within months and Sigismund was left on top.

Three men claimed to be pope. Sigismund pushed for a Church council at Constance, which met from 1414 to 1418, got rid of all three and elected a new one. It was his greatest moment. But he had given the Czech preacher Jan Hus a safe conduct to come and explain himself. The council burned Hus anyway on 6 July 1415.

When Wenceslaus died, Bohemia rose against Sigismund. The Hussites beat crusade after crusade. He was crowned emperor in Rome in 1433 and only entered Prague as king in 1436. He died in 1437 with no son, leaving his crowns to his son-in-law, Albert of Habsburg.

claims.text: Told he'd made a mistake in his Latin, Sigismund said: I am King of the Romans and above grammar.
claims.note: A famous anecdote set at Constance, recorded later. It may well be invented, but it fits his reputation.

claims.text: Sigismund let Hus burn even though he'd promised him safe conduct.
claims.note: Peter of Mladoňovice, who was there, describes the safe conduct and the arrest. The council argued a promise to a heretic didn't count.

claims.text: Sigismund blushed when Hus reminded him of his promise at the trial.
claims.note: A story told by Czech writers and repeated for centuries. It isn't in the main eyewitness accounts.

reigns.hook: Rewind to October 1410. Sigismund's election was only half the story. Days later a bigger group of electors chose his cousin Jobst of Moravia, a man with money and no scruples.
