reigns.tagline: The schemer who won the vote and died within months
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by four of seven electors
reigns.previously: Sigismund dies in 1437. Now, back to 1410 and his cousin.
paragraphs: Jobst was a nephew of Charles IV, so Wenceslaus and Sigismund were his cousins. He ruled Moravia from 1375 and gathered more land by lending money to his relatives. In 1388 Luxembourg came to him in pawn from Wenceslaus, and Brandenburg from Sigismund, which made him an elector. He was rich, clever and always scheming.

In 1394 he joined a league of Bohemian lords against Wenceslaus and had his own cousin, the King of the Romans, arrested at Prague Castle. When Rupert died in 1410, three electors chose Sigismund in September. On 1 October four others chose Jobst instead, and one of those votes was cast for Bohemia by Wenceslaus himself.

On paper Jobst had the majority. He never got to use it. He died suddenly at Brno on 18 January 1411, aged about 56, and was buried in the Church of St Thomas there. People whispered about poison. With Jobst gone, the electors lined up behind Sigismund.

claims.text: Jobst was poisoned.
claims.note: The rumour went round at the time, but there is no evidence. He was in his late fifties, old for the period.

claims.text: He had King Wenceslaus locked up in 1394.
claims.note: The lords' league seized Wenceslaus at Prague Castle, with Jobst among its leaders.

reigns.hook: Jobst's death leaves Sigismund the only king, and he rules for 26 more years. When he finally dies in 1437 he has no son, and the crown goes to his Habsburg son-in-law.

reigns.tagline: Nineteen months that handed the Habsburgs the crown
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by the princes at Frankfurt
reigns.previously: Jobst dies in 1411; Sigismund outlives him by 26 years, sonless.
paragraphs: Sigismund left a daughter, Elisabeth, and she was married to the Duke of Austria. So in 1438 her husband Albert scooped up the lot: Hungary, Bohemia, and then the German crown when the electors chose him at Frankfurt. He was the first undisputed Habsburg king since Albert I, 130 years earlier. Nobody guessed that the family would keep the title, with one short break, until the empire itself was shut down in 1806.

He never had time to enjoy it. Bohemian rebels fought him, and the Ottoman Turks were pushing up the Danube into Hungary, so that's where he spent his reign. The German princes held their Diet and talked about reform without him. In autumn 1439 dysentery swept through his army camp, and Albert died on the road home. His widow was pregnant. The son she gave birth to a few months later became known as Ladislaus Posthumous.

claims.text: Albert never once set foot in Germany during his reign as king.
claims.note: Often repeated, and his known movements were all in Austria, Hungary and Bohemia, but historians word it with care.

claims.text: After 1438, every emperor but one until 1806 was a Habsburg or married into the family.
claims.note: The single exception was Charles VII of Bavaria (1742–45). Francis I of Lorraine was Maria Theresa's husband.

claims.text: His son was born four months after he died.
claims.note: Ladislaus was born on 22 February 1440; contemporary records give the date, and his nickname comes from it.

reigns.hook: The electors need a king, fast. They settle on the dead man's cousin, a quiet, careful 24-year-old Duke of Styria. Nobody expects much from him. He'll still be on the throne 53 years later.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who won by simply outliving everyone
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Linz after a leg amputation
reigns.previously: Albert II died of dysentery in Hungary after just 19 months as king.
paragraphs: Frederick was slow, stingy and almost impossible to hurry. He held on to the German crown for 53 years, longer than any king before or after him. In 1452 he travelled to Rome, married the Portuguese princess Eleanor there, and was crowned emperor by Pope Nicholas V. No emperor would ever be crowned in Rome again.

Then he more or less vanished from Germany. For about 27 years he skipped the imperial Diets, stuck in his Austrian lands while the princes squabbled. His own brother rebelled, and in 1485 King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary took Vienna. Frederick drifted round the empire as a guest. He scratched his motto, A.E.I.O.U., on buildings, books and silver, and never explained what it meant.

Yet he kept winning. In 1477 his son Maximilian married Mary, heiress of rich Burgundy. In 1486 the electors chose Max as King of the Romans while his father still lived, and when Corvinus died in 1490 Vienna came back. Frederick's leg turned gangrenous and was cut off in 1493. He died a few weeks later, at 77.

claims.text: A.E.I.O.U. stood for “Austria is destined to rule the whole world”.
claims.note: Just one of hundreds of readings suggested since. Frederick used the letters everywhere but left no clear explanation.

claims.text: He died after eating too many melons.
claims.note: A story told by chroniclers. Old age and the after-effects of the amputation are the likelier cause.

claims.text: He was the last emperor crowned in Rome.
claims.note: Charles V was crowned by a pope later, but at Bologna in 1530; Frederick's 1452 ceremony in St Peter's was the last in Rome.

reigns.hook: Max is already King of the Romans and spoiling for a fight. The princes want something else from him: courts, peace on the roads, and a say in how the empire is run.

reigns.previously: Frederick III dies at 77, after 53 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Maximilian wanted to lead armies. The princes wanted to fix the empire. At the Diet of Worms in 1495 they made a deal: he got the promise of a tax, and they got an Eternal Public Peace that banned private feuds, plus a new imperial supreme court, the Reichskammergericht. Over the next years the empire was split into regional circles to keep order. Bits of this machinery lasted until 1806.

Max himself was always short of cash and busy fighting the French, the Venetians and the Swiss. The Swiss beat him in 1499 and drifted out of the empire for good. When Venice blocked his road to Rome in 1508, he skipped the papal coronation and simply called himself “Elected Roman Emperor” at Trent. Later emperors used the same title.

His real genius was weddings. His son Philip married the heiress of Spain, and a double wedding in 1515 lined his grandchildren up for Hungary and Bohemia. He died in 1519 before the electors had agreed on his grandson Charles.

claims.text: In 1511 Maximilian toyed with making himself pope.
claims.note: He wrote it to his daughter Margaret in a letter that survives. Whether he meant it or was joking is still argued.

claims.text: For years he travelled everywhere with his coffin.
claims.note: Later accounts say so, but no one at court recorded it reliably at the time.

claims.text: He ordered that his corpse be whipped and his hair shaved off as penance.
claims.note: His final orders asked for it. How fully they were carried out is less clear.

reigns.tagline: Half the world was his. Germany slipped away anyway
reigns.cameToPower: Won a bought election at Frankfurt
reigns.previously: Maximilian I is dead, and the electors are open to offers.
paragraphs: Charles already had Spain, the Netherlands and the Americas. The German crown cost him a fortune in bribes, mostly lent by the Fugger bank of Augsburg, and he won it in 1519. Two years later, at the Diet of Worms, a monk named Martin Luther refused to take back his books in front of him. Charles outlawed Luther, but the Elector of Saxony hid him in a castle, and the Reformation spread anyway.

Charles was away for years fighting France. In 1527 his unpaid troops sacked Rome and held the pope prisoner. In 1530 that same pope crowned him emperor at Bologna, the last papal coronation ever. In 1547 he crushed the Protestant princes at Mühlberg. Then one of his own allies, Maurice of Saxony, turned on him in 1552, and he had to flee over the Alps.

Worn out, Charles let his brother Ferdinand make the Peace of Augsburg in 1555. Each prince could now choose Lutheran or Catholic faith for his own lands. Charles then gave up all his crowns and retired to a monastery in Spain.

claims.text: At Worms, Luther declared: “Here I stand, I can do no other.”
claims.note: The words appear in early printed versions of his speech, but not in the notes taken in the hall. He may never have said them.

claims.text: Jakob Fugger reminded Charles that without his money he'd never have been elected.
claims.note: Fugger wrote it bluntly in a letter of 1523 chasing repayment. The letter survives.

claims.text: Charles held a rehearsal of his own funeral at Yuste.
claims.note: A story from later monk writers; his household's accounts don't mention it.

reigns.hook: Charles has gone to Spain to die. His brother Ferdinand, King of the Romans since 1531, finally gets the top job. Will the pope accept an emperor he never crowned?

reigns.tagline: The patient brother who made Germany's religious peace
reigns.previously: Charles V gave up all his crowns and retired to a Spanish monastery.
paragraphs: Ferdinand had done the hard work for years. Elected King of the Romans in 1531, he ran Germany whenever Charles was away, which was most of the time. He agreed the truce with the rebel princes at Passau in 1552, then the Peace of Augsburg in 1555, which his proud brother refused to put his name to. The electors met at Frankfurt in 1558, accepted Charles's resignation, and declared Ferdinand emperor.

Pope Paul IV was furious that an emperor had been made without him. Ferdinand ignored him, and no emperor ever bothered with Rome again. He spent his reign holding the Peace of Augsburg together, and pushed the Council of Trent to let Catholics take wine at communion and priests marry, hoping it would win back the Lutherans. In 1562 he got his son Maximilian elected and crowned at Frankfurt. Two years later Ferdinand died in Vienna.

claims.text: His motto was “Let justice be done, though the world perish”.
claims.note: Fiat iustitia, et pereat mundus is recorded as his motto in the 16th century, though the saying is older.

claims.text: Pope Paul IV refused to recognise him as emperor.
claims.note: The pope argued that only he could approve an emperor; his successor Pius IV dropped the quarrel.

claims.text: Ferdinand saved Vienna from the Turks in 1529.
claims.note: He held the overall command, but he was far away during the siege; the defence was led by Count Niklas Salm.

reigns.hook: The new emperor has a reputation. For years he has read Lutheran books and kept a Lutheran preacher. Rome and Madrid are watching him very closely.

reigns.tagline: The emperor nobody could pin down on religion
reigns.reignEnded: Died at the Diet of Regensburg
reigns.previously: Ferdinand I, the peacemaker of Augsburg, dies in Vienna.
paragraphs: As a young man Maximilian went to Lutheran sermons and wrote to Protestant princes as a friend. Catholics feared the next emperor would switch sides. Before his election in 1562 he had to swear to stay Catholic, and he did, more or less. As emperor he kept both camps calm and the Peace of Augsburg in one piece. Germany had a quiet decade, which was rare.

He was less lucky with the Turks. In 1566 he led a huge army to Hungary and then sat still while the fortress of Szigetvár fell. He even ran for king of Poland in 1575 and lost to Stephen Báthory. That year he had his son Rudolf elected King of the Romans, so the crown passed smoothly. In October 1576 Maximilian fell ill at the Diet of Regensburg and died there, aged 49.

claims.text: On his deathbed he refused the Catholic last rites.
claims.note: Several witnesses reported it, but Catholic and Protestant writers each spun his death their own way.

claims.text: He brought an elephant to Vienna in 1552.
claims.note: He brought it back from Spain as a young archduke; it was a sensation, and the elephant became a celebrity until it died in 1553.

claims.text: He kept a Lutheran court preacher, Johann Sebastian Pfauser.
claims.note: Pfauser preached at his court in the 1550s until Ferdinand I forced his dismissal in 1560.

reigns.hook: His son Rudolf, raised at the strict Spanish court, takes over. He's clever, moody and odd. Soon he'll pack up the whole court and move it to Prague.

reigns.tagline: Stargazers and alchemists while the empire jammed up
reigns.previously: Maximilian II died at the Diet of Regensburg, aged 49.
paragraphs: Rudolf moved the court to Prague in 1583 and filled it with wonders. The astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler worked for him. So did painters like Arcimboldo, who turned him into a portrait made of fruit and vegetables. He collected clocks, gems, rare animals and alchemists, and he suffered from deep bouts of gloom. He never married.

Meanwhile the empire's machinery jammed. Catholic and Protestant princes stopped trusting each other. In 1608 the Protestants walked out of the Diet and formed their own Union, and the Catholics answered with a League in 1609. Rudolf hardly left his castle. His brother Matthias took Hungary and Austria off him in 1608, then Bohemia in 1611. When Rudolf died in 1612 the electors had still not chosen a successor.

claims.text: Rudolf bought the mysterious Voynich manuscript for 600 ducats.
claims.note: The only evidence is a letter written in 1665, decades later, passing on what someone else had heard.

claims.text: Tycho Brahe tied Rudolf's fate to his pet lion, and the lion died just before him.
claims.note: A good story told later; no reliable source from the time links the two.

claims.text: Kepler named his star tables after him.
claims.note: The Rudolphine Tables came out in 1627, long after Rudolf's death.

reigns.hook: The electors take five months to choose. Matthias gets the crown he grabbed for at last. But he's 55, childless and tired, and the empire is splitting in two.

reigns.tagline: He fought his brother for a crown that broke in his hands
reigns.reignEnded: Died as Bohemia rose in revolt
reigns.previously: Rudolf II died in Prague, stripped of nearly all power by his brother.
paragraphs: Matthias spent years pushing his brother aside, and he finally had the empire. His chief minister, Cardinal Melchior Klesl, tried to talk Catholics and Protestants into a compromise. It didn't work. At the 1613 Diet in Regensburg the Protestant princes walked out again, and the empire's courts and assemblies barely worked.

Matthias had no children, so the family lined up his cousin Ferdinand of Styria, a hard-line Catholic. Bohemia accepted him as its next king in 1617. In May 1618 angry Protestant nobles in Prague threw two of the king's governors and a secretary out of a castle window. All three survived. Weeks later Ferdinand had Klesl arrested. The Bohemian revolt that followed started the Thirty Years' War. Matthias died in Vienna in March 1619 with everything falling apart.

claims.text: The men thrown from the window in Prague landed in a dung heap.
claims.note: Protestant pamphlets mocked them with it; Catholics said angels or the Virgin Mary broke their fall. Neither is reliable.

claims.text: The Defenestration of Prague started the Thirty Years' War.
claims.note: The Bohemian revolt that it began grew into the wider war that lasted until 1648.

claims.text: Matthias had no children.
claims.note: His late marriage to his cousin Anna of Tyrol in 1611 produced no heirs.

reigns.hook: The Bohemians want a Protestant king. The Habsburg heir, Ferdinand of Styria, heads to Frankfurt for the vote. Prague is about to give him a nasty surprise.

reigns.tagline: The Counter-Reformation emperor who set Germany alight
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Vienna, war still raging
reigns.previously: Matthias is dead and Bohemia is in open revolt.
paragraphs: Ferdinand was elected emperor at Frankfurt on 28 August 1619. Around the same time, the Bohemians deposed him as their king and chose a Protestant prince, Frederick of the Palatinate. Ferdinand struck back hard. At the White Mountain near Prague in 1620 his armies routed the rebels, and Frederick fled. He went down in history as the Winter King, and his electoral vote was handed to Catholic Bavaria.

The war spread north. Ferdinand's general Albrecht von Wallenstein raised a vast private army and beat the Danes, and in 1629 the emperor ordered the Protestants to hand back church lands taken since 1552. That Edict of Restitution scared every Protestant prince. Then Sweden's king, Gustavus Adolphus, invaded in 1630 and swept south.

Ferdinand recalled Wallenstein, then grew suspicious of him and had him killed in 1634. The Peace of Prague in 1635 settled things with most princes, but France joined in. Ferdinand died in 1637 with the war still going.

claims.text: Ferdinand said he'd rather rule a desert than a land full of heretics.
claims.note: The line is quoted in many histories, but it comes from later writers and can't be traced to a reliable source from his lifetime.

claims.text: In 1619 Austrian Protestants cornered him in the Hofburg and one grabbed his coat, until cavalry turned up just in time.
claims.note: The rescue by Dampierre's cuirassiers is real enough; the button-grabbing scene grew in later Catholic retellings.

claims.text: He approved the killing of Wallenstein.
claims.note: Ferdinand ordered him removed dead or alive; the officers who murdered him at Eger in 1634 were rewarded.

reigns.hook: His son Ferdinand, already elected King of the Romans, takes over a ruined Germany. The Swedes are still marching through it, and now the French are in the war too.

reigns.tagline: He signed the peace that let the princes go their own way
reigns.previously: Ferdinand II died with the war raging and his son already elected.
paragraphs: The new emperor had seen battle, nominally leading the victory at Nördlingen in 1634. But the war kept dragging on. The Swedes smashed his army at Jankau in Bohemia in 1645, and by 1648 they were in Prague itself, looting the castle. Peace talks had been running for years in two Westphalian towns, Münster and Osnabrück. In October 1648 the deals were finally signed.

The Peace of Westphalia changed the empire for good. Calvinists won the same rights as Lutherans. The princes could now make alliances with foreign powers, so long as these weren't aimed at the emperor. Sweden and France took land and a say in German affairs, and the Swiss and the Dutch officially left. The emperor still sat on top, but he had to work with the princes. Ferdinand spent his last years rebuilding, and in his spare time he wrote music.
His heir, Ferdinand IV, died of smallpox in 1654. When the emperor himself died in 1657, nobody had been elected to follow him.

claims.text: The Peace of Westphalia created the modern system of sovereign states.
claims.note: A popular textbook idea. Many historians now say the treaties actually strengthened the empire's own rules.

claims.text: The Swedes carried off the giant Codex Gigas, the “Devil's Bible”, from Prague in 1648.
claims.note: It's been in Stockholm ever since; the Swedish royal library holds it today.

claims.text: Ferdinand III composed music.
claims.note: Some of his sacred works and songs survive and have been recorded.

reigns.hook: Fifteen months with no emperor. France is pushing its own candidates. The Habsburgs' only hope is a teenager who was trained to be a priest: Ferdinand's younger son Leopold.

reigns.tagline: The shy music-loving emperor who outlasted Louis XIV's wars
reigns.cameToPower: Elected at Frankfurt after a long wait
reigns.previously: Ferdinand III is dead, and his heir hasn't been chosen as king yet.
paragraphs: Leopold was meant for the Church, until his elder brother died of smallpox. The empire sat without an emperor for over a year while France tried to buy the electors. They chose Leopold in July 1658, but made him promise not to help Spain. Weeks later several princes signed the Rhine League with France. The message was clear. After Westphalia, the princes did their own foreign policy.

In 1663 the Diet met at Regensburg to vote money against the Turks. It never went home. The Perpetual Diet sat there until 1806, a standing parliament of envoys arguing over seating and protocol. Meanwhile Louis XIV nibbled at the western border and grabbed Strasbourg in 1681. In 1689 French troops burned Heidelberg and wrecked the old imperial tombs at Speyer.

In 1683 the Turks besieged Vienna and Leopold fled to Passau. Polish and German armies lifted the siege that September. Leopold then turned the war round and conquered Hungary. He made Hanover a new electorate and let Brandenburg's elector crown himself King in Prussia in 1701, both in return for troops. He died in 1705 with Europe at war over the Spanish throne.

claims.text: Leopold composed music himself, including sacred works and pieces for his court operas.
claims.note: His own scores survive in Vienna, and court musicians of the day performed them.

claims.text: Leopold greeted Jan Sobieski coldly after the rescue of Vienna in 1683.
claims.note: Sobieski grumbled about the stiff meeting in letters to his wife. Leopold's courtiers worried about who should bow to whom.

claims.text: Leopold's famous Habsburg jaw was so big he struggled to close his mouth.
claims.note: His portraits show a huge jutting jaw and lip. Stories about how badly it troubled him come from later writers, not doctors.

reigns.hook: Leopold is dead and French armies sit deep inside Germany. His son Joseph, brisk and impatient, already holds the crown. He means to make the princes obey.

reigns.tagline: The young emperor who outlawed two electors
reigns.cameToPower: Already elected King of the Romans
reigns.previously: Leopold I dies with the War of the Spanish Succession raging.
paragraphs: Joseph had been elected King of the Romans as a boy in 1690, so the crown passed to him at once. He was quick, sporty and fond of women, and he wanted an emperor who gave orders. Two electors, Max Emanuel of Bavaria and his brother the Archbishop of Cologne, had sided with France. In 1706 Joseph put them both under the imperial ban, stripped of their lands and titles.

His armies did well. Prince Eugene and Marlborough drove the French out of Germany and Italy. Joseph then fought the pope over a disputed town and sent troops into the Papal States. In 1709 Clement XI gave in and recognised Joseph's brother Charles as King of Spain. The Diet readmitted Bohemia's electoral vote and confirmed Hanover as an elector. Joseph was winning.
Then, in April 1711, he caught smallpox and died at 32. He left two daughters and no son. Everything now fell to his brother Charles, still in Barcelona fighting for Spain.

claims.text: Joseph put two electors under the imperial ban in 1706.
claims.note: The ban on Bavaria and Cologne was proclaimed in Vienna. Both were restored under the peace treaties of 1714.

claims.text: As he lay dying, doctors wrapped Joseph in red cloth to draw out the smallpox.
claims.note: Red treatments were a standard remedy of the age, and accounts of his last days mention them. The details vary.

claims.text: Joseph had a string of mistresses that worried his pious mother.
claims.note: Court letters and diplomatic reports discuss his affairs openly. His biographer Charles Ingrao covers them.

reigns.hook: Joseph is dead and his brother is the only Habsburg male left. If Charles becomes emperor and King of Spain, he'll be as mighty as Charles V. His allies start to panic.

reigns.tagline: The emperor who spent 30 years buying signatures
reigns.reignEnded: Died after a bad meal, so they say
reigns.previously: Joseph I dies of smallpox, leaving only daughters.
paragraphs: Charles came back from Barcelona to be elected emperor in October 1711. His allies took fright. Britain didn't want a Habsburg ruling Spain and the empire at once, so it made a separate peace with France at Utrecht. Charles fought on alone, then gave up. The peace of 1714 left Spain to Louis XIV's grandson. Charles got the Spanish Netherlands, Milan and Naples, and the Bavarian elector got his lands back.

Charles had no son. His answer was the Pragmatic Sanction, a family law letting his daughter Maria Theresa inherit the Habsburg lands. He spent decades getting Europe to sign it. In 1732 the Diet guaranteed it, though Bavaria, Saxony and the Palatinate voted no. To win France over, he let Lorraine go. The Duke of Lorraine, Maria Theresa's husband, was given Tuscany instead.

His last wars went badly. He lost Naples and Sicily, then lost Belgrade to the Turks in 1739. In October 1740 he fell ill after a hunting trip and died within days. His daughter could inherit Austria. A woman couldn't be emperor, though, and the electors were free to choose.

claims.text: A dish of mushrooms killed Charles VI.
claims.note: Voltaire wrote that a pot of mushrooms changed the history of Europe. He did eat them before falling ill, but the cause of death is uncertain.

claims.text: Prince Eugene said a full treasury and a strong army would guard the Pragmatic Sanction better than treaties.
claims.note: The remark is widely quoted. No reliable record shows him saying it in those words.

claims.text: The Imperial Diet formally guaranteed the Pragmatic Sanction in 1732.
claims.note: The Diet's vote is on record, along with the protests of Bavaria, Saxony and the Palatinate.

reigns.hook: Charles is dead and no Habsburg man is left to elect. The Elector of Bavaria, married to Joseph I's daughter, smells his chance. So does the new King of Prussia.

reigns.tagline: Crowned emperor just as his own capital fell
reigns.cameToPower: Elected with French and Prussian help
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Munich, beaten and broke
reigns.previously: Charles VI dies. A woman can't be emperor, so the throne sits empty.
paragraphs: Charles Albert, Elector of Bavaria, was married to Joseph I's daughter. He never accepted the Pragmatic Sanction. In 1740 Prussia invaded Silesia, France joined in, and Charles saw his chance. He marched on Prague and had himself crowned King of Bohemia. In January 1742 the electors chose him as emperor. He was the first emperor outside the Habsburg family in three centuries.

He was crowned in Frankfurt on 12 February 1742. The next day Maria Theresa's troops marched into Munich. The new emperor had lost his own capital. He stayed in Frankfurt, living on French money, an emperor with almost no lands. Austrian soldiers plundered Bavaria. Without Habsburg wealth behind it, the imperial title turned out to be mostly a fancy hat.

In 1744 Frederick of Prussia attacked Austria again and Charles got Munich back. He didn't enjoy it for long. Sick with gout and worn out, he died there in January 1745, aged 47. His son made peace within months and promised his vote to Maria Theresa's husband.

claims.text: Wits turned the motto 'aut Caesar aut nihil' (Caesar or nothing) into 'et Caesar et nihil': emperor and nothing.
claims.note: The joke is often quoted about him. Who made it first, and when, isn't clear.

claims.text: Austrian troops entered Munich the day after his coronation.
claims.note: Contemporary reports and military records agree on the dates: crowned 12 February, Munich occupied 13 February 1742.

claims.text: France paid for his court and his war.
claims.note: French subsidies kept him going. Historians such as Peter Claus Hartmann have traced the payments.

reigns.hook: The Bavarian emperor is dead and his son wants out. Maria Theresa can't wear the crown herself. But her husband can, and she has the votes lined up.

reigns.tagline: The emperor whose wife held the real power
reigns.previously: Charles VII dies in Munich, his empire in pieces.
paragraphs: Francis Stephen had given up his home duchy of Lorraine to marry Maria Theresa, getting Tuscany in exchange. In September 1745 the electors made him emperor. The crown came back to the family, but Maria Theresa ran Austria, Bohemia and Hungary. She refused to be crowned empress. Francis had the title, and she had the armies and the money. Everyone knew who decided.

Francis found his own job. He was a gifted businessman who ran the family's finances, invested in factories and lent money to the state. He collected rocks and natural wonders, and started the menagerie at Schönbrunn. In the empire, the Seven Years' War split Germany. The Diet declared war on Prussia, and in 1757 Frederick routed the imperial army at Rossbach.

In 1764 Francis got his son Joseph elected King of the Romans, so the next reign was safe. A year later, at their son Leopold's wedding in Innsbruck, Francis collapsed and died. Maria Theresa wore black for the rest of her life.

claims.text: Maria Theresa watched Francis's coronation from a window and led the crowd in cheering.
claims.note: Witnesses describe her cheering from a balcony in Frankfurt. The details grew in the retelling.

claims.text: Francis did business with the enemy, supplying goods that reached Prussia's armies.
claims.note: Rumours said so during the Seven Years' War. His dealings were complex, and proof is thin.

claims.text: Goethe, then 14, watched Joseph's coronation in Frankfurt in 1764.
claims.note: He described the ceremony at length in his memoir 'Dichtung und Wahrheit'.

reigns.hook: Francis is dead. Joseph is emperor at 24, bursting with ideas. But his mother still holds every Habsburg land, and the empire's princes have no wish to be reformed.

reigns.tagline: The reformer the German princes ganged up against
reigns.previously: Francis I collapses at his son's wedding in Innsbruck.
paragraphs: Joseph became emperor in 1765 but his mother kept the Habsburg lands. So he started on the empire. He sent inspectors to the supreme court at Wetzlar, which had a mountain of unfinished cases. The review dragged on for years and achieved little. He travelled Europe under a false name, Count Falkenstein, and loved being treated like an ordinary man.

Joseph wanted Bavaria. When its elector died in 1777, he moved in troops. Frederick of Prussia marched to stop him. The 'Potato War' of 1778 had almost no battles; the armies mostly dug up spuds. In 1785 Joseph tried again, offering to swap Belgium for Bavaria. Frederick formed a League of Princes against him. The German princes now trusted Prussia more than the emperor.

After his mother died in 1780, Joseph rushed through reforms in his own lands, and they provoked revolts in Hungary and Belgium. Ill with tuberculosis, he cancelled many of them. He died in February 1790. His brother Leopold had to come up from Tuscany to pick up the pieces.

claims.text: Joseph wrote his own epitaph: here lies a ruler who meant well but failed in everything.
claims.note: The line is often quoted, but there's no grave inscription and versions of it differ.

claims.text: Soldiers in the War of the Bavarian Succession spent more time foraging for potatoes than fighting.
claims.note: Both armies lived off the land. The nicknames 'Potato War' and 'Plum Fuss' come from the soldiers themselves.

claims.text: The young Goethe trained at the Wetzlar court during Joseph's inspection.
claims.note: Goethe was there in 1772, and the summer gave him the setting for 'The Sorrows of Young Werther'.

reigns.hook: Joseph is dead and Europe is jumpy. In Paris, the Bastille has fallen. The electors meet in Frankfurt to crown his calm, clever brother Leopold.

reigns.tagline: The wise fixer who had no time left
reigns.previously: Joseph II dies with Hungary seething and Belgium in revolt.
paragraphs: Leopold had ruled Tuscany for 25 years, and ruled it well. In 1786 he abolished the death penalty there, the first state in Europe to do so. He came north in 1790 and calmed things down fast. He made a deal with Prussia and soothed the Hungarians. In autumn the electors chose him as emperor, and he was crowned in Frankfurt in October 1790. By December his troops had taken back Belgium.

Revolutionary France was the trouble. The French had abolished the rights of German princes who held land in Alsace, and the princes demanded the emperor act. French nobles fled to the Rhineland, begging for an army. Leopold's sister was Queen Marie Antoinette. In August 1791 he and the King of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, saying they would act only if the other powers joined in.

Leopold meant it as a threat on paper. In Paris it sounded like a plan to invade. He was still hoping to avoid war when he fell suddenly ill and died on 1 March 1792, aged 44. Seven weeks later France declared war on his son.

claims.text: Leopold was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours blamed French revolutionaries, among others. His doctors' reports point to illness, and no proof of poison exists.

claims.text: Tuscany under Leopold was the first state to abolish the death penalty.
claims.note: His penal code of 30 November 1786 did it. Tuscany still marks the date.

claims.text: The Declaration of Pillnitz was meant as an empty threat.
claims.note: Its wording made action depend on other powers agreeing, which was unlikely. The French took it as a real threat all the same.

reigns.hook: Leopold is dead and France is spoiling for a fight. His son Francis is 24, dutiful and cautious. He'll be the last man ever crowned Holy Roman Emperor.

reigns.tagline: The last Holy Roman Emperor, who shut it all down
reigns.previously: Leopold II dies suddenly. Revolutionary France wants a fight.
paragraphs: Francis was crowned in Frankfurt on 14 July 1792, the last coronation of a Holy Roman Emperor. France was already at war with Austria. Over the next ten years French armies beat him again and again. In 1797 he secretly agreed to give up the Rhine's left bank. In 1803 the Diet carved up the old church states and most free cities to pay off the princes who'd lost land. A thousand years of maps vanished.

In 1804 Napoleon made himself Emperor of the French. Francis worried his own title might not last, so he declared himself Emperor of Austria too. Then came Austerlitz in December 1805. Napoleon's German allies grew into kingdoms. In July 1806 sixteen princes formed the Confederation of the Rhine under Napoleon and announced they were leaving the empire.

Napoleon told Francis to give up the crown. On 6 August 1806 he did, and he declared the empire dissolved. No Diet voted on it. The crown jewels stayed in Vienna, where you can still see them. Francis went on as Emperor of Austria until 1835, and even married his daughter to Napoleon.

claims.text: Voltaire mocked the empire as neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.
claims.note: He wrote it in his 'Essai sur les mœurs' in 1756. Historians today think the joke is unfair to how the empire really worked.

claims.text: Francis had no legal right to dissolve the empire on his own.
claims.note: Lawyers argued he could abdicate but not abolish the Reich. Nobody was in a position to stop him.

claims.text: Francis became the 'double emperor', holding two imperial titles at once from 1804 to 1806.
claims.note: His proclamation of 11 August 1804 created the Austrian title while he kept the old one.
